lesson_title: The Day the Queues Stretched for Kilometres
hook_text: In 1994, millions of South Africans stood in line for hours, and many of them had waited their whole lives for this day.
clip_script: 1991. Leaders who had been enemies for decades sit down at one long table. They argue. The talks collapse. Outside, the violence is terrible. Boipatong. Bisho. Then, in April 1993, Chris Hani is shot dead outside his home. The country holds its breath. Mandela goes on television: stay calm, he says, don't let them win. The leaders set a date. Right-wing gunmen invade a homeland. Bombs explode. Inkatha joins just one week before the vote. And then, on 27 April 1994, it happens. Grandmothers. Students. Farmers. Workers. Black and white, standing together in queues that stretch for kilometres. Many are voting for the first time in their lives. On 10 May, Nelson Mandela becomes President. 27 April is now Freedom Day.
visual_style: A long negotiating table at Kempton Park; newspaper headlines about violence; candles at a memorial for Chris Hani; a television showing Mandela's address; endless queues of voters of all races; an elderly woman holding up her ballot; Mandela taking the oath at the Union Buildings.
pacing: Rapid and anxious through the crises, slowing into a triumphant finale.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to understand the negotiations, the violence and the democratic election of 1994.
